resources.string: Did you know that eating a healthy diet can improve fertility and better prepare your body for pregnancy? What you eat plays a very important role in your overall health and should never be taken lightly…

What Is a Healthy Diet?
Did you know that eating a healthy diet can improve fertility and help prepare your body for pregnancy? This means that your daily meals should be chosen carefully and with proper understanding.
A healthy diet, also known as a balanced diet, includes the right amounts of all the major food groups your body needs to function well and stay strong.
If you are unsure whether your current diet is healthy, do not hesitate to speak with a doctor or nutrition professional. Together, you can create a weekly meal plan that supports your health and pregnancy goals.
What to Eat and What to Avoid
Many diets have been medically proven to support good health. Some healthy food choices include:
• Fruits such as pineapple, watermelon, apples, berries, oranges, mangoes, and bananas • Starchy foods like potatoes, millet, yam, oatmeal, bulgur, and whole-wheat bread • Protein sources such as lean meat (excluding liver), chicken, eggs, seafood, beans, and lentils • Healthy oils (in moderation), including olive oil, vegetable oil, and oils found in fish, avocado, and nuts • Plenty of clean drinking water
Foods and drinks you should try to avoid include:
• Fish that contain high levels of mercury, such as bluefin tuna, swordfish, shark, and mackerel • Foods and drinks containing caffeine, including tea, chocolate, energy drinks, and soda. Daily caffeine intake should not exceed 200 milligrams • Refrigerated pâté, smoked seafood, or processed meat spreads • Herbal products that have not been medically approved • Alcohol, in any amount • Unpasteurized juice, milk, soft cheeses, and similar products
Choosing a healthy diet is an important step toward a safe pregnancy and long-term wellbeing.

Kí ni Oúnjẹ Tó Dáa?
Ṣé o mọ̀ pé oúnjẹ tó dára lè túbọ̀ mu ìbímọ́ rọrùn, kí ó sì pèsè ara rẹ dáadáa fún oyun? Èyí túmọ̀ sí pé oúnjẹ tí o ń jẹ lojoojúmọ́ yẹ kí o jẹ́ pẹ̀lú ìmúlòye àti àyẹ̀wò dáadáa.
Oúnjẹ tó dáa, tí a tún ń pè ní oúnjẹ tó dájú, ni oúnjẹ tí ó ní ìwọ̀n tó péye lára gbogbo ẹgbẹ̀ oúnjẹ pàtàkì tí ara ènìyàn nílò fún ìlera, agbára, àti ìdagbasoke.
Tí o bá ń ṣiyèméjì bóyá oúnjẹ tí o ń jẹ dára tàbí kò dára, má ṣe ṣiyèméjì láti bá dókítà tàbí amọ̀ja oúnjẹ sọ̀rọ̀. Pẹ̀lú ìtóju wọn, o lè ṣètò àtòjọ oúnjẹ ọ̀sẹ̀ kan tó máa ràn ara rẹ lọ́wọ́ dáadáa.
Ohun Tí O Yẹ Kí O Jẹ àti Ohun Tí O Yẹ Kí O Yàgò Fún
Ọ̀pọ̀ irú oúnjẹ ló wà tí ìmọ̀ ìṣègùn ti fìdí rẹ̀ múlẹ̀ pé wọ́n dára fún ara ènìyàn. Àwọn àpẹẹrẹ ni:
• Eso bíi oyinbo, elegede, àpù, eso kékeré, ọsan, mango àti ogede • Oúnjẹ sitashi bíi poteto, oka ilẹ̀, iṣu, oatmeal, bulgur àti burẹdi alikama gidi • Amuaradagba bíi ẹran tí kì í ní ọra púpọ̀, adìẹ, ẹyin, ẹja omi, ẹ̀wa àti lentili • Òróró tó dára (ní ìwọ̀n tó péye), bíi òróró olifi, òróró ẹfọ́, àti òróró inú ẹja, avocado àti èso igi • Omi mímu tó mọ́, púpọ̀
Àwọn ohun tí o yẹ kí o gbìyànjú láti yàgò fún ni:
• Ẹja tí ó ní mercury púpọ̀, bíi bluefin tuna, swordfish, shark àti mackerel • Oúnjẹ àti mímu tí ó ní caffeine, bíi tii, ṣọ́kọ́lẹ́ẹ̀tì, mímu agbára àti soda. Kò yẹ kí caffeine ojoojúmọ́ ju miligiramu 200 lọ • Pate tí a fi sínú firiji, ẹja tàbí ẹran tí a ti sun tí a fọ́ sílẹ̀ • Àwọn ohun èlò ewé ìwòsàn tí kò tíì ní ìtẹ́wọ́gbà ìṣègùn • Ọtí, ní ìwọ̀n kankan • Omi eso, wara, warankasi rọrùn àti àwọn oúnjẹ tí a kò tíì paṣítọ́ọ̀sì
Yíyan oúnjẹ tó dáa jẹ́ ìgbésẹ̀ pàtàkì sí ìlera rere àti oyun aláàbò.

Many women worry about the physical changes that happen during pregnancy. Some even delay getting pregnant because of these concerns. While these changes are natural and differ from one woman to another, there is no reason to feel ashamed of your body.

Many women feel anxious about the physical changes that occur during pregnancy. Some even postpone pregnancy because of these worries. Although these changes are natural and vary from woman to woman, there is no reason to feel embarrassed or ashamed of your body.
Learning to accept these changes can help you feel more confident and maintain healthy self-esteem throughout pregnancy.
Pregnancy occurs in three main stages known as trimesters: • First trimester: conception to 12 weeks • Second trimester: 13 to 27 weeks • Third trimester: 28 to 40 weeks
Each trimester brings its own physical and emotional changes.
During the first trimester, your baby’s body begins to form, and vital organs start developing. At the same time, your body undergoes significant adjustments. You may experience nausea, fatigue, frequent urination, and emotional ups and downs.
Hormonal changes during this stage can be intense, especially for first-time mothers, and may cause mood swings and discomfort.
As your breasts begin to enlarge in preparation for breastfeeding, wearing a supportive bra becomes important. Veins on the breasts may become more visible, and choosing loose, comfortable clothing can help reduce discomfort.

Ọ̀pọ̀ obìnrin máa ń ṣàníyàn nípa ayípadà ara tí yóò ṣẹlẹ̀ nígbà oyun. Diẹ̀ ninu wọn kì í ṣe kó tó débi pé wọ́n máa ń fi oyun sílẹ̀. Bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ pé ayípadà wọ̀nyí jẹ́ adayeba, kò sí ohun tí o yẹ kí o fi tiju ara rẹ.

Ọ̀pọ̀ obìnrin máa ń ní ìbànújẹ̀ tàbí ìbẹ̀rù nípa ayípadà ara tí yóò ṣẹlẹ̀ nígbà oyun. Diẹ̀ ninu wọn kì í ṣe kó tó débi pé wọ́n máa ń dá oyun dúró. Bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ pé ayípadà ara wọ̀nyí jẹ́ adayeba, wọ́n sì ń yàtọ̀ láti ọ̀dọ̀ obìnrin kan sí omíì, kò sí ìdí kankan láti fi tiju ara rẹ.
Gbigba ayípadà ara rẹ gẹ́gẹ́ bí apakan ìrìnàjò oyun lè mú ìgboyà ara ẹni pọ̀ sí i, kí o sì ní ìmọ̀lára rere nípa ara rẹ.
Oyun ní àkókò mẹ́ta pàtàkì tí a ń pè ní trimester: • Àkókò kìnní: láti ìbímọ́ dé ọ̀sẹ̀ kejìlá • Àkókò kejì: láti ọ̀sẹ̀ kẹtàlá dé ogún-dín-lọ́gbọ̀n • Àkókò kẹta: láti ọ̀sẹ̀ kọkànlá-dín-lọ́gbọ̀n dé ogójì
Pẹ̀lú ọkọọkan àkókò wọ̀nyí ni ara obìnrin máa ń ní ayípadà tirẹ̀.
Ní àkókò kìnní, ara ọmọ inú bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í dá sílẹ̀, gbogbo àwọn ara pàtàkì rẹ̀ sì ń dá sílẹ̀ díẹ̀ díẹ̀. Ní àkókò kan náà, ara ìyá tún ń ṣe àtúnṣe púpọ̀. O lè máa ń rí ìrora inú, ìrẹ̀wẹ̀sì, ìlọ sí ilé ìgbònsẹ̀ lọ́pọ̀lọpọ̀, àti ayípadà ìmọ̀lára.
Àwọn homonu ara máa ń pọ̀ sí i ní àkókò yìí, èyí sì lè fa ayípadà ìmọ̀lára àti ìbànújẹ̀, pàápàá jùlọ fún àwọn tí wọ́n ń loyun fún ìgbà àkọ́kọ́.
Bí àyà ṣe ń túbọ̀ pọ̀ sí i ní ìmúrasílẹ̀ fún mímu ọmọ, ó ṣe pàtàkì kí o lo bra tó dára tó sì lè fún ọ ní àtìlẹ́yìn. Àwọn ẹ̀jẹ̀ inú àyà lè hàn kedere sí i, nítorí náà yíyan aṣọ tó túbọ̀ rọrùn àti tó tobi díẹ̀ lè jẹ́ ìrànlọ́wọ́ púpọ̀.

🌍 Cervical Cancer: Global Facts & Prevention
Cervical cancer affects over 660,000 women every year and causes nearly 350,000 deaths, mostly in lower-income countries. It’s mainly caused by long-term infection with HPV types 16 and 18.
What helps prevent it? • HPV vaccines before sexual activity • Regular screenings (Pap smears, HPV tests) • Healthy habits like not smoking
With action, we can save lives. Let’s close the gap between rich and poor countries and eliminate cervical cancer globally.

🚨 Don’t Miss These Signs
Cervical cancer doesn’t always show symptoms early on, which makes screening so important.
Watch for: • Bleeding between periods or after sex • Unusual vaginal discharge • Pelvic pain or discomfort during sex
Real stories remind us: speak up, get checked, and don’t ignore your gut feeling. Early detection saves lives.

Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide, with over 660,000 new cases and nearly 349,000 deaths in 2022. It disproportionately affects low- and middle-income countries—those with a low Human Development Index (HDI) experience twice the incidence and five times the mortality compared to high-HDI countries.
The primary cause is a persistent infection with high-risk HPV types 16 and 18, responsible for approximately 70% of cases. Most HPV infections resolve naturally, but chronic infections can lead to precancerous lesions.
Prevention strategies include: • HPV vaccination (e.g., Gardasil 9 or Cervarix) before sexual debut to dramatically reduce risk • Screening methods such as Pap smears, high-risk HPV testing, and visual inspection (especially in low-resource settings) • Maintaining safe sexual practices, not smoking, and adopting a healthy lifestyle
Without intervention, the global burden of cervical cancer is projected to rise to approximately 760,000 new cases and 411,000 deaths by 2030.
